explanations.explanation: That's the question, friend. The king asks, "Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given to you." (Esther 7:2). He asked her something like this at her first banquet (Esther 5:6), and the text says he asks "once more." I think he's curious what could be so big that she needed two banquets to say it.

Good guess, because that invite is the real mystery in the room. But the king never asks about it. He asks, "Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given to you." (Esther 7:2). Haman's seat at the table stays quiet for now, and I think the king is more interested in her answer.

Her people are the heart of her answer, but the king doesn't ask where anyone is from. He asks, "…what is your petition?" and offers "Even up to half the kingdom…" (Esther 7:2). Esther is the one who brings up her people, asking for "…the lives of my people…" (Esther 7:3). That's a big difference, friend.

explanations.answer: Her life and her people's lives
explanations.explanation: That's it. She says, "…grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request." (Esther 7:3). Half a kingdom was on the table, and she asked for lives instead. Nobody at that table could miss what she was asking for.

explanations.answer: A palace and servants of her own
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but she doesn't ask for property. The king offered "Even up to half the kingdom…" (Esther 7:2). What she asks for is this: "…grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request." (Esther 7:3). It's a request for lives.

explanations.answer: A seat on the king's council
explanations.explanation: I get why that sounds like a queen's kind of ask. But in this verse she doesn't ask for a job or a title. She says, "…grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request." (Esther 7:3). It's a request for life, and it covers her people too.

Yep. Esther says, "If we had merely been sold as menservants and maidservants, I would have remained silent…" (Esther 7:4). She says it wouldn't justify burdening the king. What she's facing is "…destruction, death, and annihilation." which is a whole different size of problem.

This one's actually True, friend. Esther says, "If we had merely been sold as menservants and maidservants, I would have remained silent, because no such distress would justify burdening the king." (Esther 7:4). She's telling him this is far worse than servitude. The stakes are "…destruction, death, and annihilation."
Right on the money. Esther says, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked man—Haman!" (Esther 7:6). No hint, no maybe. She names the man who dined at her banquet. That took some nerve, friend.

Bigthana is one of the king's officers who plotted against him. Mordecai reported that plot (Esther 2:21-23), and later the record of it is read to the king (Esther 6:1-3). But Esther doesn't name him here. She says, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked man—Haman!" (Esther 7:6).

Teresh was the other officer in that old plot against the king, alongside Bigthana (Esther 2:21). Different story, friend. Esther's answer is plain: "The adversary and enemy is this wicked man—Haman!" (Esther 7:6).
That's the word. "…Haman stood in terror before the king and queen." (Esther 7:6). Esther had just named him as the enemy. I think his wine suddenly didn't taste so good.
No big speech from Haman here. The text says he "…stood in terror before the king and queen." (Esther 7:6). Nobody's squaring up or arguing back, friend. I think he just realized how bad things were.
Relief would be quite a twist, but not this time. Esther names him, and Haman "…stood in terror before the king and queen." (Esther 7:6). Nothing good for him is coming out of that moment.

Yes. "In his fury, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden…" (Esther 7:7). The text gives us his fury and where he went. It doesn't tell us why he went out there. Esther had just named Haman as the enemy (Esther 7:6).

I can see why sorrow came to mind, with so much heavy news in that room. But the text names a different feeling: "In his fury, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden…" (Esther 7:7). Fury is the word the text uses for the king. That comes right after Esther names Haman, friend.

The king has plenty to think about, but confusion isn't the word. "In his fury, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden…" (Esther 7:7). Esther just told him exactly who the enemy was. He knows who, and now he's furious.

explanations.answer: Begs Queen Esther for his life
explanations.explanation: That's right. Haman "…stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he realized that the king was planning a terrible fate for him." (Esther 7:7). The woman he was plotting against is now the one he's begging. I'd call that a rough turn, friend.

explanations.answer: Slips out through a side door
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a side door, friend. It says Haman "…stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life…" (Esther 7:7). He knew the king had a terrible fate planned for him, and he stayed put in that room.

Zeresh, Haman's wife, did give him advice earlier (Esther 5:14). But in this scene he doesn't send for her. He "…stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life…" (Esther 7:7). It all happens right there at the banquet.

This one is False, friend. The king says, "Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?" and then the text says, "As soon as the words had left the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face." (Esther 7:8). The text doesn't show Haman explaining himself, only his face being covered. Things moved fast.

Right. The king says, "Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?" and "As soon as the words had left the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face." (Esther 7:8). The text shows Haman's face covered, not Haman speaking. I think that covering is a sign things were going badly for him.

That's him. Harbonah says the gallows was built "…for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king." (Esther 7:9). Mordecai is Esther's cousin (Esther 2:7), and Haman had the gallows built for him. Now that very gallows comes up in front of the king.

Hegai was the king's eunuch who looked after the women in the palace (Esther 2:8). But he doesn't come up in this verse. Harbonah says the gallows was built "…for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king." (Esther 7:9).

Hathach was one of the king's eunuchs, appointed to attend Esther, who went out to Mordecai for her (Esther 4:5-6). He's not the man here, friend. Harbonah says Haman built the gallows "…for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king." (Esther 7:9).

Yes. Harbonah speaks up, and the king declares, "Hang him on it!" (Esther 7:9). The gallows was at Haman's house. The text says they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai (Esther 7:10).

This one is True, friend. After Harbonah mentions the gallows, "Hang him on it!" declared the king (Esther 7:9). The king gave the order himself. The gallows Haman built for someone else is the one they use.
